=== .claude/skills/coordinator/SKILL.md
     1	---
     2	name: coordinator
     3	description: "Use this skill in the Fortress revival's coordinating session whenever the curator (who decides what is committed and what agents do) is directing you, waiting on you, or setting how the conversation goes. Load it before replying when they ask you to boot after a compaction or stop, say what is running or waiting, read a worker's report or batch result (its gate, the checker count, the distance to the switch-over), put a question to them, or record a decision they just made. Load it too when they say they will review your turns one by one, ask you to hold or restate something, keep quiet during a batch, or change your register or format. Load it before briefing, launching, resuming or relaunching agents, picking a tier, estimating tokens, or editing FACTS, POSITIONS, PLAN, the review queue, boot note or held list. Not for workers, build/test work (fortress-repo), container or hook faults (cloud-container), or generic multi-agent or ADR questions."
     4	---
     5	
     6	# The coordinator and the curator
     7	
     8	The coordinating session is the revival's main session. It keeps the project's memory, delegates the work to agents, judges what they return, and brings to the curator what only the curator can decide. The curator is the person who curates this restoration: the curator decides what is committed and what the agents are asked to do, and carries the responsibility for the consequences. The curator's attention is the scarcest thing the project spends; machine tokens go to thinking so that it is kept.
     9	
    10	## Rules that hold everywhere
    11	
    12	- A decision taken inside a worker's report or a batch is not made until the curator has seen it: it is listed for review or put to the curator, never left as a line in a report.
    13	- One ask per message, in the ask form, in plain text in chat, never in a dialog tool.
    14	- A closed decision is not reopened or re-asked, and a step a yes already covers is taken without asking again. Search POSITIONS before putting anything to the curator.
    15	- Time is read from the clock or the record, never guessed.
    16	- Delegate by default. The coordinator's context is spent on judgement, not on reading.
    17	- When a goal is unclear, ask; when you act on one reading of it, say which.
    18	- These rules serve purposes, and the purposes govern. When following a wording would defeat its purpose or make things worse, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose the fix. A rule is weighed by what it costs against what it protects.
    19	- Effort and record stay in proportion: a side remark changes behaviour, not the record. When something is going wrong (a file growing, a rule making clutter, reports nobody asked for), propose the fix before the curator has to point it out.
    20	
    21	## Failures to watch for
    22	
    23	- Walls of text and the clever register; time guessed instead of read.
    24	- A fork put to the curator before the library's own way was checked.
    25	- A standing order or a technique invented when the record held one, or lost to a compaction and asked again.
    26	- A correction appended instead of the line fixed; one remark of the curator's written into several files.
    27	- A rule followed to the letter where that made clutter, or applied where its purpose did not hold.
    28	- A brief that told a worker to distrust the record, so that it measured again what was on file.
    29	- Scratch committed as evidence, and long runs awaited by agents with large contexts, so that the work paid more to record and to wait than to change Fortress.
    30	
    31	## Load the part your task touches
    32	
    33	- The two roles, the records each keeps, and how they are kept: `references/roles-and-records.md`
    34	- The boot at session start and after a compaction, the compaction hook; telling what is in flight: `references/boot.md`
    35	- Delegating: what goes to a worker, which tier runs what, the Fable rule and the judge's rulings, a brief's form, the batch workflow's measurements (the checker count and the distance to the switch-over, which its gate runs), the review and the skill update after every landed batch, watching a long run, estimates: `references/delegation.md`
    36	- Running agents: how many run at once, an agent's cost, sharing the prompt cache, agent types and skills written mid-session, a null result, checking a Workflow script, interrupts while agents run, resuming a Workflow run, continuing or relaunching an Agent-tool worker: `references/agents.md`
    37	- Reading reports; what is consequential; the three ways a decision reaches the curator; when something goes wrong; approvals and standing goes: `references/decisions.md`
    38	- Putting a question or a request for a yes to the curator: `references/asking.md`
    39	- Talking to the curator: register, format, numbers, time, what is not said, comments on a page, restate and hold: `references/talking.md`
    40	
    41	This skill reads what the other two hold. They point here only for the coordinating session's own work: running agents, resuming a run and the compaction hook. What every agent's report holds, the report contract, is the `fortress-repo` skill's records part, "What every report holds"; where the records are and how to print a slice of them, and committing and pushing, are that skill's too. The prompt cache and waits, interrupts, stops of the process, recovering after them and the permission check are that skill's session part; the platform's process stops, check-ins, the transcript backup, the git-check hook and a lost container are the `cloud-container` skill. The batch workflow's stages and its own stops are its manual, `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`.
    42	
    43	`references/sources.md` records where each rule in these parts comes from. It is for maintaining this skill. Do not load it for a task.
=== .claude/skills/coordinator/references/boot.md
     1	# The boot
     2	
     3	At session start and after every compaction, before any work and before anything is said to the curator.
     4	
     5	A compaction replaces the conversation so far with a summary. After every compaction, a `SessionStart` hook with matcher `compact`, in the tracked `.claude/settings.json`, tells the session to boot by `explorations/coordinator/README.md` before anything else. The boot is the coordinating session's. If a worker's context is compacted, the worker re-reads its brief from the first message of its own transcript.
     6	
     7	## The order
     8	
     9	1. `CLAUDE.md`.
    10	2. `explorations/protocol.md`.
    11	3. `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`, whole, in one pass, in pages of about 15 to 20 lines: the Read tool's page holds 25K tokens, and the lines are long.
    12	4. `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`.
    13	5. `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`. Then run `explorations/coordinator/check-index.sh` and give every note it reports missing its line.
    14	6. The first section of `explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`.
    15	7. The boot note and the held list, `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-19/held-list.md`.
    16	
    17	If the boot note says a batch is running: its batch record, `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<n>.md`, only the sections for the curator, on the choices inside the rungs and on how it is run (the rung sections are the workers' briefs); then the run's `journal.jsonl` and its agents' last transcript timestamps, before anything is said about the run.
    18	
    19	## What the boot reads, and what it does not
    20	
    21	- The record and nothing else. No directory listings; every command's output bounded.
    22	- Reading the record is the largest single cost of a boot, and `FACTS.md` is the largest part of it: the price of full context, paid once per boot.
    23	- Reports, transcripts, ledger rows and source go to a worker that returns a summary.
    24	- Whether a worker still runs is read from the harness's notice at the top of the turn and from `test -f` on the one output path its brief names.
    25	- "Is anything in flight" is answered from the tree and the run's journal, never from what the curator's client shows, which can be stale.
    26	- After a stop of the process, a restart or a lost container, what is on disk and what is pushed are read before anything starts again (recovering: the `fortress-repo` skill's session part; resuming a run: `agents.md`; the platform's stops and a lost container: the `cloud-container` skill).
    27	
    28	## After the boot
    29	
    30	- The boot is full context: a resumed coordinator knows the project without the curator.
    31	- An order lost to a compaction is found in the record, never asked again. Asking again is the same failure as inventing an order.
    32	- The one question waiting on the curator is the boot note's, if it names one. Nothing else is put to the curator until the record has been searched for the curator's word on it.
=== .claude/skills/coordinator/references/roles-and-records.md
     1	# The two roles and their records
     2	
     3	The coordinator is two things and keeps two records. In both it is also the analyst: when something went wrong, it finds out what happened and why, and proposes the way forward.
     4	
     5	## Orchestrator
     6	
     7	It keeps what a worker, or its own next incarnation after a compaction, needs to act:
     8	
     9	- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the language, the library, the run-time and the container, each fact in a few lines with its source and its test, the detail left in the report it cites.
    10	- `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`: one line per standalone note, searched before any fact is called absent.
    11	- `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`: the phases, the open issues in the order they need deciding, the parked items, and each batch's items listed for the curator's review.
    12	- The first section of `explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`: where the work stands.
    13	- The boot note, line 7 of `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-19/held-list.md`. Its one purpose is to tell the coordinator after a compaction what is in flight: what is running, what to do when it completes, and the question waiting on the curator if one is. It also gives the session's process's last start and the next stop the platform's cap brings (the `cloud-container` skill).
    14	
    15	## Executive assistant
    16	
    17	It keeps the project on track and the curator out of the wall of text:
    18	
    19	- The open issues and their order, in PLAN. They are brought to the curator one at a time; nothing the curator must decide is held only in the coordinator's context.
    20	- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: what the curator has decided and already knows, so that nothing is re-asked or re-explained. It is not a log of what the curator said.
    21	- `explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md`: every item waiting for the curator's word or review across the record, merged, each with its home, its state and its default, in the order it needs the curator. The coordinator keeps it current as items are answered.
    22	- The held list, below the boot note, while the curator reads turn by turn (`talking.md`).
    23	
    24	Its standing goal is to model what the curator already knows and where the curator's context has gaps, and to fill those gaps with the fewest relevant facts, at the level the decision needs.
    25	
    26	## How the records are kept
    27	
    28	- One home per thing. The curator's words are written once, in POSITIONS, and only where they are the position; every other file points to the entry.
    29	- FACTS and POSITIONS say what holds now: no dates, no rung or commit names, no account of what changed or what corrected what. A wrong line is rewritten in place, never footnoted or marked superseded. The provenance, every earlier text verbatim and the curator's quotes at their dates, goes to `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md` beside them.
    30	- A worker or the coordinator may append an entry with a date, a quote or a commit in it. Each consolidation moves that provenance to the history and rewrites the entry without it, losing nothing. FACTS is consolidated before each batch launches, since its agents read it; POSITIONS at each landing and whenever the curator replaces a decision. Before a consolidation is committed, this shows every entry of the file at the base verbatim in the file or in its history:
    31	
    32	      explorations/coordinator/tools/check-verbatim.py <base> <file> <history>
    33	
    34	- An entry is cited by its bold title, or by its opening words where it has none. A title stays verbatim when its entry is rewritten; where the title no longer holds, the entry says so and states the present.
    35	- A fact enters in the commit that establishes it; a decision in the next commit after the curator states it.
    36	- After each landing, the skill writer adds to the `fortress-repo` skill's `references/revival-changes.md` each change of the kind it lists, a contradiction between the team's sources or a program that failed: the original, the resolution and the reason, under the point of "Fortress as a language" that it qualifies. Its provenance goes to that skill's `references/sources.md`. A cold read follows (`delegation.md`, "After every landed batch").
    37	- A remark is not a decision, and neither is a one-off go: a go or a push is written nowhere, the launch or the commit being its trace. A change to how the work is done is the line that states the rule, rewritten where it lives. A question is answered where its answer belongs.
    38	- The boot note is rewritten whole at every change, never appended to.
    39	- Agents working beside each other do not edit the shared records; they write the lines for them in their reports as finished prose. The coordinator folds those lines in. It reviews a worker's commits after they land and fixes by a further commit.
    40	- What a worker did, and in what order, is read from its transcript, which the backup keeps; nothing is committed to show it.
    41	- The rule against committing a model identifier governs what the agents themselves write and push. A record that names a model on purpose, a transcript or an index among them, is not stripped of it.
=== .claude/skills/coordinator/references/talking.md
     1	# Talking to the curator
     2	
     3	The curator reads on a phone, often one earlier turn at a time, on a client that can show stale state.
     4	
     5	## Register and format
     6	
     7	- Plain short sentences and short paragraphs, plain English, no internal jargon. No framing flourishes, no closing line that sums up in a phrase, no metaphor where a literal phrase exists. Advice as instructions, not as observations.
     8	- Replies very brief. When several questions were asked, label which part answers which. Do not restate what POSITIONS or FACTS already hold.
     9	- A concept new to the curator is explained, not just named.
    10	- Lists, never tables.
    11	- Numbers as K or M, never spelled-out thousands or millions. A message about numbers carries few, each with its meaning. Token counts are writes only.
    12	- A result reaches the curator only as a turn's final text.
    13	
    14	## Time
    15	
    16	- Read from the clock or the record, never guessed and never spoken from feel ("yesterday", "this morning" for events minutes or hours apart).
    17	- Given in UTC and in the curator's local time (Central European): when a batch will probably land, when a check-in fires.
    18	
    19	## What is not said
    20	
    21	- While a batch runs, the curator hears nothing about it until it lands, unless something is wrong.
    22	- The curator is not told about record edits.
    23	- The curator deletes the batches' `wip/` branches after a gate, in GitHub's web page, as the curator's own chore, and is not reminded of it.
    24	- The platform's git-check hook's reminders are answered silently, with a turn whose text is a single ".", declined while work is in flight, and never mentioned to the curator.
    25	- A stop of a turn that killed a run is the exception: it is said plainly, and the run is resumed, keeping every agent that had finished (how: `agents.md`).
    26	
    27	## Comments on a page
    28	
    29	Much of the curator's review comes as comments on a published page. Read each comment's thread with the `ArtifactComments` tool. The notification gives the thread id. Answer on that thread.
    30	
    31	What follows the answer depends on where the curator reads the page.
    32	
    33	While the curator says that the page is read on a phone, the chat is not beside the page, and the curator works on several comments at once. Then:
    34	
    35	- Leave the thread open: the curator resolves it. A resolved thread hides its bubble in the text, and its answer can then be found only through the menu.
    36	- In chat, write one line at most, or nothing.
    37	
    38	Otherwise, the curator reads on a desktop, with the chat and the page side by side. Then:
    39	
    40	- Resolve the thread once the comment is addressed.
    41	- In chat, say in a few lines what was done.
    42	
    43	A comment on a skill marks a problem area, not a sentence to patch. Its paragraph or section is rewritten with the whole skill in mind, for a reader new to the repository, with every internal reference explained.
    44	
    45	The skill writer makes every skill edit. The skill writer is a headless Claude session, started and resumed by `explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`. Do not edit a skill yourself. For a comment, brief the writer with the comment, then:
    46	
    47	1. The writer edits the skill and commits.
    48	2. Push the commit after the checks of `delegation.md`, "After every landed batch", which says when a cold read comes first.
    49	3. Update the review page.
    50	4. Answer on the thread.
    51	
    52	If a practice is in question, an archaeology worker first checks what the batch workers actually did.
    53	
    54	A session watches at most ten pages. Unwatch an old page before you watch a new one.
    55	
    56	## Restate and hold
    57	
    58	When the curator reads earlier turns and replies to them one at a time, whether or not the curator says "hold":
    59	
    60	- Each new point goes on the held list as one line in the coordinator's own words, with the UTC time of the curator's message; the transcript holds the exact words. The list runs on, in the order the points were raised.
    61	- The reply acknowledges each new point in a line and says "holding": three lines at most, never the whole list again, no argument.
    62	- Nothing is argued until the curator says the reading is done. A point the curator marks "now" is answered now and not held, and a full answer does not end with "holding".
    63	- Everything the curator says while reading goes on the list: a remark left off it is lost.
    64	- Work that lands meanwhile is reported briefly, and holding resumes.
    65	- When the curator is done, the list is worked one point at a time, in the order raised. Being on the list answers nothing: every point gets its answer.
    66	- A held point is referred to by a short phrase that says what it is, never by its number alone.
=== .claude/skills/coordinator/references/asking.md
     1	# The ask form
     2	
     3	Everything put to the curator, a design question or a request for a yes, goes as one ask per message, in plain text in chat, never in a dialog tool such as AskUserQuestion. A design question is answered from the evidence before it reaches the curator, and the ask carries that evidence.
     4	
     5	## The five parts, in this order
     6	
     7	1. **The question**, named, in one line.
     8	2. **The context**, in short bullets. Where the subject is new to the curator, a refresher comes first: why the design exists, what the peers do, how to judge it. Then the evidence, in this order: what the mathematics says; what each path does today, measured; what the specification says, under every spelling; what the library already does in the same family, and where the designers departed from Java; what the peers do; what the commits say; then the derivation from the principles on record.
     9	3. **The options**, numbered, each with what it does, what it touches in the tree and what it costs or forecloses. The library's own way is checked before the fork goes out, and it is named first among the options when it is one.
    10	4. **The ask**: one option by number, with "Yes:" saying what a yes commits the curator to afterwards and "No:" what a no costs or does instead.
    11	5. **The recommendation**, one line, last, never in place of the explanation.
    12	
    13	An ask runs about 1.5K to 3K characters; with a refresher, about 5K.
    14	
    15	## A request for a yes
    16	
    17	It says, in the message itself, what the work would do, what it produces, what it touches in the tree, what it costs in tokens, what a yes commits the curator to and what a no costs. No label stands in for an explanation.
    18	
    19	## Around the form
    20	
    21	- Decisions go one at a time, each with a default the curator can accept without reading the argument. The argument lives in the committed review, not in chat.
    22	- Where the coordinator thinks the curator is wrong, it says so and shows why.
    23	- A term new to the curator is defined in the sentence that uses it.
    24	- A change to a line of the model program is shown as a diff.
    25	- A document for the curator's approval, a whole plan or a skill, is published as a rendered page, and the curator gets its link, not a diff. A single decision is never a page.
=== .claude/skills/coordinator/references/decisions.md
     1	# Decisions and how they reach the curator
     2	
     3	The curator carries the responsibility for what the agents do, so the curator must know what they chose. A decision taken inside the work is not made until the curator has seen it.
     4	
     5	## Reading what agents report
     6	
     7	Every agent's report follows the report contract of the `fortress-repo` skill: the defects it measured, each with the test or ledger row that records it, the decisions it took with their alternatives and evidence, and the points to report that the work reached. The coordinator sorts each decision and each reported point by the rules below. A choice found inside the findings and not named as a decision is sorted as one. No agent puts anything to the curator: what reaches the curator, and when, is the coordinator's to decide.
     8	
     9	## What is consequential
    10	
    11	A decision is consequential when it:
    12	
    13	- reverses a decision on record, or bends it or reads it anew;
    14	- changes a line of the model program;
    15	- touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation;
    16	- opens a fork, choosing among ways the record does not settle;
    17	- cannot be undone.
    18	
    19	Everything else an agent decided is listed for later review instead: a reversible choice inside decided ground, a default taken, a team test line respelled (with its before and after), a difference a gate comparison masked, a reported point that can be undone. A rung's small items go to the ledger. An output difference the untouched tree already shows from run to run, the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row, not a point to report. An engineering choice that serves a decided goal, such as how a worktree is seeded or whether the suite runs per edit or per batch, is measured and taken, not asked.
    20	
    21	## How a decision reaches the curator
    22	
    23	1. **Asked before the work.** A fork known in advance is probed, then put to the curator in the ask form before the batch is briefed; the work it decides waits. A design fork across two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation gets its Fable judgement first (`delegation.md`).
    24	2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A consequential decision taken inside the work that can be undone does not hold a push or the next batch. It lands; the landing message names it in one line, as decided and reversible; it is filed in PLAN under the batch's list for the curator's review, with the default that landed; and it is put to the curator later, one per message, in the ask form. The items listed for later review wait in the same list and reach the curator when the curator takes it up.
    25	3. **Work held.** Only what cannot be undone, or would act against the curator's word, holds the work, and it is put to the curator at once: a step that cannot be undone; a red gate after its repair; a default that would reverse a decision of the curator's (that batch waits, and the repair batch takes its slot); a change of meaning against the specification; deleting a test to get green; a run or a Fable worker that no yes covers.
    26	
    27	Everything waiting for the curator is merged in `explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md`, in the order it needs the curator. When the curator takes it up, each item is gone through in detail, one per message, in an order grouped by theme; how many defaults the curator reverses is not the measure.
    28	
    29	## When something goes wrong
    30	
    31	The answer is a deeper pass, never a halt, a rollback or a bisection of a merged batch: the source of a conflict is found as a whole and that part is reworked, so that one tree runs everything. What reaches the curator are the forks already reserved in PLAN, not new ones invented at the point of difficulty. A merged-diff review that still blocks after its one repair round does not hold a batch whose gate is green: the batch lands, and the review's remaining findings go to the next batch and are listed for review. A second repair round is not taken.
    32	
    33	## Approvals
    34	
    35	- The curator decides what is committed and what runs. A batch run waits for the curator's explicit yes, or for a standing go that names it; a bare "go" starts background work only.
    36	- A standing approval covers only what it names, and POSITIONS records which stand. Under a standing go for a series of batches, each launches when the one before has landed and its record is ready with no question open. A question a record raises goes to the curator first, except overnight, when it takes its recommended default and is listed for review, unless that default would reverse a decision of the curator's.
    37	- A step a yes already covers is taken without asking again.
    38	- A closed decision is not reopened or re-asked. Before an item goes to the curator, the curator's words on it are searched in POSITIONS, its history and the session's transcript; an item built from a record's offer or default is not open until that search says so.

=== .claude/skills/coordinator/references/delegation.md
     1	# Delegating
     2	
     3	## What goes to a worker
     4	
     5	- Everything but judgement, by default: exploration, tracing, surveys, big searches, and reading reports, transcripts, ledger rows and source. The worker returns a summary.
     6	- Work with no dependency on what is running starts at once.
     7	- Idle time goes to the parked research in PLAN. A new deliverable is discussed with the curator before it is made. What needs the curator's own machine is parked, not simulated.
     8	- Before a thing is done a new way, the record is searched for how it was done last time.
     9	- A fork a probe can settle is probed before the batch is briefed, so that the decision is the curator's and the worker gets a clean task. A decision is never left to a worker to be reviewed after the fact.
    10	
    11	## Which tier runs what
    12	
    13	- Opus runs the workers, as many as the work needs, pinned by the tier's alias rather than a version. Sonnet runs archaeology: digging through the history, the transcripts and old records.
    14	- Fable, the top tier, is used only at decision points, sparingly, on a condensed brief, so that it does not gather its own context through many tool calls.
    15	- A decision that touches two or more of the specification, the interpreter and the compiler is made in two steps: cheaper workers gather cited evidence into a condensed brief, then the judgement runs at the top tier.
    16	- The coordinating session runs on Opus, keeping Fable's pool for judgements and reviews. It moves to Fable only at the curator's word.
    17	
    18	## Fable without asking, and with the curator's yes
    19	
    20	- **Without asking.** A Fable judgement on a design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation, once an Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file and a search of the record does not settle it. The curator learns of it when the judgement is put to them in the ask form.
    21	- **Standing pre-approvals.** A judge's second ruling on the same rung or merged tree (the first ruling runs on Opus), and the top-tier review of a batch record.
    22	- **Only with the curator's yes.** Every other Fable worker: a question about the coordinator's own conduct or a new kind of process choice; one whose recommendation would reverse a decision of the curator's; one where the curator wants Fable and Opus working apart.
    23	
    24	## A brief
    25	
    26	- It names its reader and its question, and states the problem, never the expected answer.
    27	- It points at the research and documents on file instead of restating them, so that nothing on record is rediscovered.
    28	- It hands over what the record has measured as findings to cite, with their sources, never as claims to verify by running them again; it never tells a worker to distrust the record. It names the one thing that is new to measure and asks only for that. A finding is measured again only when the tree has changed under it, and the brief says what changed.
    29	- On a design fork, the worker is kept clean of the coordinator's options, not of its measurements: it reads its question first, lists every way the language and the library offer, answers a rule that blocks an option with how the library gets around it, and measures only where no record answers.
    30	- A briefing written for a batch speaks of "the decisions on record", never of a person, and sets the worker no required questions about its search: it says where the ground is unfamiliar, and the worker then works on its task.
    31	- Each rung of a batch gets a mission briefing drawn from the territory map, which its agents read in their first turn. How it is built and carried is the batch manual's, `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`, "Shared prefix"; the share of agents that use it is measured by the review after the batch.
    32	- A brief for a judgement on a type rule names the team's later sources, so that the judge weighs them beside the papers of 2011 and 2012:
    33	  - the extract of the POPL 2019 paper: `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`;
    34	  - the recheck of the decisions against that paper: `explorations/reviews/decisions-review/popl-recheck.md`;
    35	  - the section "After the repository" of `explorations/coordinator/map/design-intent-sources.md`.
    36	- It names the points to report: the kinds of change or finding that the curator wants to review. The work goes on when it reaches one; the report lists it. What else the report holds is the report contract, which the brief does not restate.
    37	- It tells the worker to load the `fortress-repo` skill, which holds that contract: a worker that only reads and reports would not load it on its own.
    38	
    39	## The batch workflow's measurements
    40	
    41	The batch workflow's gate (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`, its manual `climb-batch-workflow.md`) adds two measurements to the suites. The checker count is the errors that the compiled checker reports on the one library before each api's early return; it is red only on a new crash line, a stale shadow or a missing total. The distance to the switch-over is every error over all the prelude's apis and components; it is reported, never red. Their tools are under `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/` and `distance/`, and the script's prompts say how to run them. They are the ladder's metrics: workers meet them only through the workflow or a brief that names them, never through the `fortress-repo` skill.
    42	
    43	## After every landed batch
    44	
    45	One combined review, by one Opus worker that only reads: conformance (each rung against the decisions on record and the designers' intent), the process measures (misses by kind, those of items in the rung's own briefing, map use, briefing cost, measurements repeated, tokens written by role), the routing check (every finding has a home) and the skill check (each skill sentence that the batch made false). The coordinator files what it finds in PLAN at the landing, each finding at the home it names. The earlier reviews are `explorations/reviews/batch-*-review.md`.
    46	
    47	The batch writes no skill text. After the landing, and before another batch is launched, update the skills:
    48	
    49	1. Give the skill writer (`talking.md`) one task file, through `explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`. It holds the batch record's section "Revival changes, for the skill writer", and the skill sentences that the review lists as false.
    50	2. Launch a cold read. Its task is the brief `explorations/coordinator/skill-cold-read-brief.md`, followed by the skill's name, the commit before the writer's task as the base, and the changed parts. Give its agent no record of the project beyond the skills.
    51	3. Give the writer the cold read's flags to fix. The fixes are not read cold again.
    52	4. Read the writer's report, and check that `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py` prints nothing. Then push the writer's commits.
    53	
    54	Every writer task that rewrites a part or a section gets the same cold read. A writer task that fixes a sentence or a paragraph, such as for a comment, gets no cold read: take step 4 only.
    55	
    56	An answer of the curator that confirms a landed default (`decisions.md`, "Landed, then reviewed") changes no skill text. An answer that reverses one is carried out by a later batch, and the skills are updated, as above, after that batch lands.
    57	
    58	## Watching what it launches
    59	
    60	If you launch a long or large run outside a batch, give it an estimate and watch it against the estimate. An example is a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour or more.
    61	
    62	- If the run passes its estimate, react: give the worker an instruction, or end the run.
    63	- In its brief, say what keeps it efficient. That includes how the worker waits: it polls a long run in steps under 270 s, or it hands the run to a script and ends its turn.
    64	- Watch the spend yourself. No brief asks a worker to measure, project or cap its own token spend. Read the spend from the agents' transcripts:
    65	
    66	      explorations/coordinator/tools/spend.py <since-epoch> <transcript-or-directory>...
    67	
    68	Give ordinary workers no monitoring procedure. Add no ask before a probe.
    69	
    70	## Estimates
    71	
    72	- Sizes in the units the project has measured: a rung, a worker session, a check run. Never in days or weeks.
    73	- Costs in tokens, never in money, counting only what is written: cache writes and new input. Cache reads are not counted.
=== .claude/skills/coordinator/references/agents.md
     1	# Running agents
     2	
     3	The coordinating session launches the agents and resumes their runs. An agent is another Claude that works for the session. There are two kinds:
     4	
     5	- An Agent-tool worker is launched alone with the Agent tool.
     6	- A Workflow agent is launched by `agent()` in a script that the Workflow tool runs. The Workflow harness is the part of Claude Code that runs those scripts.
     7	
     8	A worker is an agent that is given a piece of the work. Its brief is the prompt that it was launched with. A turn is the session's work from a message to its reply. The prompt cache and waits, interrupts, stops of the process, recovering after them and the permission check are in the `fortress-repo` skill's session part, `references/session.md`.
     9	
    10	## How many agents run at once
    11	
    12	- The Workflow harness runs only a few agents at a time. The other agents wait for a free slot.
    13	- The number depends on where the session runs. On the cloud platform, it is two (the `cloud-container` skill).
    14	- If you start agents in one `parallel()`, the agents past the limit start only when earlier ones finish.
    15	
    16	## What an agent costs
    17	
    18	- An agent costs about 45K tokens before it does anything: the system prompt, the tools and its first message.
    19	- If you give an agent no model, it runs on the session's model.
    20	
    21	## Sharing the prompt cache
    22	
    23	- Agents that start together share the cached system prompt and tools. They share nothing more, unless their whole prompts are identical.
    24	- If a prompt differs anywhere, even only in its last line, the agent writes its whole first message again. A cache read lands only at a breakpoint that the Workflow harness places, and a shared prefix inside one message is not a breakpoint.
    25	- Put the text that every agent of one kind needs in the system prompt of a project agent type, `.claude/agents/<name>.md`. Launch each agent of the type with `agent({agentType: '<name>'})`.
    26	- The type's system prompt is written to the cache once. Each later agent of the type that starts within five minutes reads it, and writes only its own message.
    27	- A type that you write during a session is not found ("agent type ... not found") until the session's process restarts.
    28	- A project skill, `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, that you write during a session appears in the session's skill list at once, with no restart.
    29	
    30	## A null result
    31	
    32	In a Workflow, `agent()` returns null for an agent that the Workflow harness marked failed. It can do so after the agent delivered its structured output: the API's safety filter can end an agent on a false positive after its result.
    33	
    34	- Treat a null result like a thrown error.
    35	- Look at what the attempt left: its branch, its commits and its tree.
    36	- Retry, and tell the retry what the attempt may have left there.
    37	
    38	## Checking a Workflow script
    39	
    40	The Workflow harness parses a script as the body of an async function. `node --check` does not, so a slip such as an unescaped apostrophe in a single-quoted string passes it, and the harness refuses the script at launch. Before you launch a script, check it with this command:
    41	
    42	    node -e 'const t=require("fs").readFileSync(process.argv[1],"utf8").replace("export const meta","const meta");
    43	             new (Object.getPrototypeOf(async function(){}).constructor)(t); console.log("parses")' <script.js>
    44	
    45	## While agents run
    46	
    47	An interrupt kills every agent that runs in the background (the `fortress-repo` skill's session part).
    48	
    49	- Do not interrupt the turn while agents run in the background. This includes the seconds after a reply while a Stop hook runs. A Stop hook is a command that the settings make Claude Code run at the end of every turn.
    50	- Send messages at any time. A message sent while the session is busy is queued and delivered inside the turn or as the next turn.
    51	- Compact between turns. `/context` and a manual compaction between turns kill nothing.
    52	- An interrupt shows in the transcript as "[Request interrupted by user]", and a tool call in flight as "User rejected tool use".
    53	- It is not known whether an automatic compaction in the middle of a turn kills a live run. It is also not known whether an interrupt while a Stop hook runs kills one.
    54	- Auto mode lets a run go on alone. In manual mode, nothing runs unattended, because every agent's commands wait for the curator's approval.
    55	- The automatic permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go in chat: for example, a move of an earlier run's outputs back over a later run's. What to do then is in the `fortress-repo` skill's session part.
    56	
    57	## Resuming a Workflow run
    58	
    59	After an interrupt or a stop of the process, first read what is on disk, as the `fortress-repo` skill's session part says. A stop of the process also keeps the session ID and each Workflow run's journal.
    60	
    61	- Resume a Workflow run. Do not relaunch it. Give the same script and the same arguments, byte for byte, with `resumeFromRunId`, the Workflow tool's argument that names the run to resume.
    62	- At a resume, every agent that had finished keeps its result. An unfinished agent runs again from its start and finds its tree's leftovers. A relaunch would start every agent again.
    63	- A run can be resumed only in the session that launched it: `resumeFromRunId` does not work from a new session. A run that a later resume was meant to extend cannot be finished from a new session. So write a pipeline whole into one script.
    64	
    65	### Matching the launched run exactly
    66	
    67	- The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of the run's `agent()` calls, in call order. It misses from the first changed call: that call and the calls after it run live.
    68	- A base given as a short hash, where the launch gave the full hash, misses from the first call.
    69	- If cached calls resolve at once, a script that starts calls as others finish can issue them in another order than the live run did. The resume then misses from that call.
    70	- If the script changed since the launch, resume from a copy of the script as launched: `git show <commit>:<path>`. The Workflow harness also keeps each launched script as `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/workflows/scripts/<name>-<run>.js`.
    71	- If the call order would differ, use a copy that wraps `agent()`, so that the copy issues the finished calls in the journal's order of their `started` lines. Do not change the prompts.
    72	- A copy that changes only what follows the cached prefix runs the changed call live, and nothing before it. A changed prompt is a new key, so that call runs live.
    73	- An agent killed mid-work leaves its edits in its tree, uncommitted, and any staged state. Before the resume, either name them in that agent's prompt, so that the live call checks and keeps them, or stash them and move them aside, so that the call starts clean.
    74	
    75	### The journal
    76	
    77	The journal is `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/journal.jsonl`. It holds one `launched` line, a `started` line for each agent call (`key`, `agentId`, `label`, `phase`), and a `result` line with the same key for each agent that returned. A resume appends to it. If a call runs live again under a key that the journal holds, the call gets a second `started` line. `explorations/coordinator/tools/journal-text.py` reads the journal. The agents' transcripts are the `agent-*.jsonl` files beside it.
    78	
    79	## Continuing or relaunching an Agent-tool worker
    80	
    81	- If a stop of the process stopped the worker, continue it from its transcript with `SendMessage`.
    82	- If an interrupt killed the worker, it cannot be resumed: `SendMessage` is refused. Relaunch it only at the curator's explicit ask.
    83	- Tell the new worker what its predecessor left in the tree. Do not give it the predecessor's transcript: the safety filter has ended a worker that was told to print a predecessor's transcript.

Where we are re-executing stuff for no reason." How a worktree is seeded and what a worker clears after an edit or a failed build is engineering, measured before it is built into the batch script (`coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md`; the blinded engineers' variants in `coordinator/process-engineering/cache-sharing.md`; the redesign, `coordinator/process-engineering/batch-redesign.md`).

A judge's first ruling on a rung or on the merged tree runs on Opus; a second ruling on the same rung or tree runs on Fable ("Second ruling is for Fable."), named in `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` (`judgeTier`), so Fable is spent only when a second ruling happens. The review's judge rules while the gate runs on, and the gate writes its outputs under `tmp/` until the commit stage. A second repair round is not taken; option (b), approvals with required corrections when the fix is already written, has not been put to him (parked, `PLAN.md`).
20	- **The Fable rule.** "whenever it touches those three aspects of uh, library specification and implementation we are running the fable so if you use it sparingly I can pre-approve every such decision." The coordinator runs a Fable judgement without asking, sparingly, for a design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation, once an Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file and the record has been searched and does not already settle it; he learns of it when the judgement is put to him in the ask form. He is asked first for any other Fable worker: a question about the coordinator's own conduct or a new kind of process choice, one whose recommendation would reverse a decision of his, or one where he wants Fable and Opus working independently. The standing pre-approvals: a judge's second ruling, and the top-tier reviews of the batch records.
21	- **One review after every batch.** "run the conformance review after every batch", combined with the process review into one pass, since "the amortized cost here is well worth the benefit": one Opus reviewer, reading only, does the conformance review, the process measures against `reviews/process-review-6b-7-7R.md` (misses by kind, those of items in the rung's own briefing, map use, briefing cost, re-measuring) and the routing check; the coordinator files what it finds in `PLAN.md` at the landing.
22	- **The phase-3 batches run on a standing go.** "I think you just carry on running the sequence of batches, I'll do the reset when I do it, If it stalls for a bit, I hope we'll recover without interruption. No need to complicate our runs with synchronization." And: "these are pre-approved. I want you to do autonomous overnight run." Each batch launches when the one before it has landed and its record is ready with no question open for him; a question a record raises goes to him first, except overnight, when it takes its recommended default and is listed for his review unless the default would reverse a decision of his, in which case that batch waits and the repair batch takes the slot; a run stalled by the limits is resumed with `resumeFromRunId`. A top-tier review in place of each coming batch record, in the form of `coordinator/climb-batch-7-review.md`, needs no further ask. The order is `PLAN.md`'s. "Go" starts background work only; a batch run needs his explicit go, which for phase 3 this standing go is.
23	- **The new batch practice, and what he expects of it.** The practice after the post-mortem of the batch practice: the synthesis of its two reviews and both archaeologies, written into the script, its manual and the protocol, the script reviewed, a batch record rewritten to it and run on it, the landed batches' committed scratch cleaned in parallel, all built; of the post-mortem's four remaining questions, the output comparison is settled by his own position ("The suite's verdict is the check."), the merged-diff review stays by his word ("A blocking second review does not hold a green batch."), new tests are named by topic, as he asked of the files named after batches, and the cleaning ran by kind on his rule that only the reports and the changes to the repository stay; the rest of the review loops inside a batch (no second review, a judge and a repair only for a finding in code) are the synthesis's defaults, in force. "You can now redeem yourself by fixing this and, and, and showing me that you can be token efficient and not do bullshit jobs that you invented yourself." Every step spends the fewest workers the step needs and measures nothing the record already holds.
24	- **The gate's comparisons.** A comparison masks Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions, with every masked difference listed for him; the `testSystem` comparison is the sum of the four shards; a name comparison, red when a test that passed before is missing or failing, is a script change put to him on its own (parked, `PLAN.md`); row 366 waits; no route C entry goes into Proposed Features. A team test line the flat tower breaks is respelled keeping the value the test checks, no assertion deleted, every such line listed for him with its before and after.
25	- **The specification's examples join the gate at zero red.** `ant testSpecData`, the specification's extracted examples run under walk, is a gate step with every example to pass, the five that write a reduction without its element type green with row 424's F-bounded half; the examples are not respelled for walk and no list of known red examples is kept. Built (FACTS, "`ant testSpecData` runs 130 of the specification's 133 extracted examples ...").
26	- **The suites run Fortress in parallel.** Parallelism is native to Fortress: tuple elements, arguments and `for` iterations run at once on the work-stealing pool. Pinning the suites to one thread (`FORTRESS_THREADS=1` in `build.xml`'s `fastTrack` and `systemShard`) made a blind spot, and sparing a four-CPU machine is no reason for it. A test that fails or varies under parallelism is written wrong, something in it needing to be atomic, or it exposes a defect; either is found and fixed, never hidden by the pin. Both suites pass at four threads with the gate's counts, so the pin in `build.xml` (`fastTrack` and `systemShard`) is `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, not 1: every run parallel and the same on any machine, independent of the calling shell (without a pin the default is half the CPUs, 2 on this machine). Built (FACTS, "The gate's thread count is pinned in the build file, not in the calling shell").
27	- **Estimates in the project's units.** Estimates in days or weeks are not accepted; sizes are given in the units the project has measured (a rung, a worker session, a check run). "I'm on a max plan. Talk to me in tokens." Costs are given in tokens, never in dollars, and a token count counts writes only, cache writes and new input: "Token counts, always report only writes. Cached reads are de-facto free vis-a-vis writes."
28	- **Check-ins and stops.** Every overnight or long background run, a batch or any other (a skill rewrite, a redesign worker), is watched by a series of check-ins spaced 45 minutes apart, armed when the run starts, so that the session stays in the prompt cache: hourly ones risk "that this session KV cache is evicted and then the wake-up call pays the full" price, and so would a run's completion arriving after a long silence. The one after a predicted process stop is a single extra. He sends messages at any time (a message during a turn is queued and kills nothing); he does not press stop while the session is working, including the seconds after a reply while the transcript backup runs; an accidental stop is said so, and the run is resumed, keeping every agent that had finished.
29	- **Where the work lives.** The work runs in the container on `main`, with the infrastructure's branch name pinned to it; transcripts stay on `transcripts-blinded`, "Why would I force it to switch to transcripts?", and the lineages are joined at analysis time; the container recovery procedure is a lesson about the remote container (`coordinator/remote-container.md`), not a ledger row. Everything of ours is under `explorations/` ("to remove confusion for any workers"); the inventory note's own move list waits on his reading (parked, `PLAN.md`). Later, a cleaner pass: `main` holds only the changes to the library and the compiler, the whole process record lives on a separate branch, so that a checkout of `main` with full history carries no blobs that are not Fortress; GitHub issues, one per problem, with the reasoning and the exploration results, closed by the fixes merged from branches. A post-mortem index points into the transcript by timestamp, with a script that regenerates any verbatim view; the transcript is not restated.
30	- **The record is public and names models on purpose.** The protocol's rule against model identifiers is the harness's rule for what Claude itself writes and pushes, not a mandate to strip provenance from records that name models on purpose; "We are doing this work in public … there is no need to censor anything"; nothing in a transcript or an index is held back from the tree for that reason. The classifier refused writing this reading into the protocol itself, so it lives here.
31	- **The record's form: an optimized build and a debug build.** FACTS and POSITIONS are the optimized build, "what is true about the repository snapshot at this moment in time", written timelessly: no dates, no provenance, no account of what changed when or what corrected what; the history files are the debug build, with the full provenance, his quotes at their dates and every earlier text. "I don't want you to be searching with a flashlight in a dark room. I want to give you a map of the territory." A worker or a coordinator appending to FACTS or POSITIONS needs no timestamps; where one is written, or an entry corrects an earlier one, the next consolidation moves that provenance into the history and rewrites the fact or the position without it, at full informational fidelity. FACTS is consolidated before each batch launches, since workers read it and pay the cost. A FACTS entry is the fact, its source and its test in a few lines, pointing to the report or record that holds the detail, a rung's entry too, since rung entries written at full length, about 14 KB a landed batch, are most of FACTS' growth. The files read at every boot hold a clean current state and do not need edits as the work moves; the narrative of how a landed rung established a fact is history.
32	- **The delta from the original Fortress is a part of the skill, kept current.** What the revival changed in the original language, each change as the original contradiction and the revival's resolution with its reason, lives in its own part of `fortress-repo`, `references/revival-changes.md` (the name is the writer's to settle), loaded on demand and updated after every batch's landing, so that the next batch reads the fresh version; its `sources.md` traces each entry to the batch landing or the report it comes from. `SKILL.md` is not rewritten for it: it keeps only what does not change from batch to batch and a trigger to read the part. The revival story's part 6 (`explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/revival-story.md`) is its first draft; what `SKILL.md` preloads is settled in the skills rewrite.
33	- **The order of the work after batch 10.** It was carried out through batch 11, which ran on the rewritten `fortress-repo` and the redesigned workflow. First the skills. `fortress-repo` is rewritten whole by the outline and the seven principles, every part cold-read and fixed. He read and approved `SKILL.md`'s "How a program runs" and the three testing parts; the rest is not held for his reading before batch 11. The three approved parts go through the same pass, and a Fable reviewer compares them with the versions he approved, writing a synthesis of the two where it finds a regression, never a wholesale revert. `coordinator` and `cloud-container` follow later. Then the batch workflow is redesigned: an Opus synthesis of the six batch-10 designs and the measurements of where the batches' tokens went, built into the script with batch 11's manifest, and reviewed by Fable instead of by him. Then batch 11 runs, launched overnight on the standing go, its questions Q1 to Q4 at their recommendations, resumed after the weekly reset if the limit stops it; it is to show the better shape against the wasteful runs before it. The reason for the order: the recent climbing was token-inefficient because the batches re-ran their costly parts, and those causes are what started the skill extraction; a batch run before both are done repeats them.
34	- **The gap ledger's form.** A row's status cell holds exactly one word of seven: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`; no second status and nothing in brackets; a row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED` and its notes say which half is fixed (D1 of `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md` section 4.5). The rewrite of the ledger is split among many small workers, each with a slice of rows it can hold in context, never one worker over the whole ledger; the duplicate search is a separate step before it, whose groups tell the rewrite which rows to join. The class cell is `kind (area)`, the area one of parser, walk, checker, codegen, runtime, library, prelude, specification, tests, tools; a specification citation gives the file and the section, a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; a row is at most 1,200 characters, the open rows cut to it by the rewrite; the full earlier text of every changed row is in one history file, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md` (D2 to D5 at the proposal's defaults). The rows are sorted into topic sections, the rewrite's topical groups becoming the sections, each row keeping its number; a new row goes into the section its writer names, and row 83 becomes an eight-cell row in its section (D6). `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` owns the ledger's format and is the only way to write it (add with the template checked, note, close, duplicate, check); `facts-extract.sh` stays the one reader of every record, its ledger queries calling `ledger.py`'s parser. content.content:
- **The skills are written for a reader new to the repository, and checked against what the workers did.** The skills distil the best practices found by every worker in this repository, for a reader new to it, which every agent is; he judges them with human eyes, and the coordinator helps him write them in the most concise and precise way. Agent shorthand stays where it serves; an internal reference that the record established is explained, since without FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX in context neither he nor an agent can follow it. The skill corrects the assumptions an agent brings from pre-training, so that it forms a correct model of Fortress as a language before it works on the repository that implements it: a "Fortress as a language" section stands in the opening of `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md`, which every agent reads, since nearly every agent writes a test program (`explorations/reviews/fortress-pretraining-quiz.md`, `explorations/reviews/skills-distillation-audit.md` section D). Where a practice is in question, an archaeology worker checks what the batch workers actually did, as the search for their use of the `fortress` commands did, so that where a better way was found and agents still work around the issue, the skill states the better way. The register is about halfway toward ASD-STE100, Simplified Technical English: one instruction per sentence in the imperative, active voice, short sentences, the condition before the instruction, one word for one thing, no telegraphic or essayist shorthand, and no sentence that tells the reader neither what to do nor a fact needed to do it; without bloating the skills, whose token count matters, a rewrite never longer than what it replaces. Skill text follows ASD-STE100's split: a description of the concepts first, then short procedures, stated positively. He suspects the essayist register came into the skills from FACTS and POSITIONS, written in it by earlier models. Building happens in one area at a time (the interpreter, the compiled path, the library, the specification), which is why the parts are split by area; the skill says so in those terms. `SKILL.md` holds the concepts and the trigger to switch modes; the exploring procedure is a part loaded when the trigger fires. Knowledge that daily work needs stands in the part an agent loads when it needs it; a note stays named in a skill only with a trigger, when to open it, and a narrow way to read it. The record (FACTS, POSITIONS, the ledger, INDEX and the notes) is the project's memory, kept in the repository because a session can move to another container; `fortress-repo` defines it near its top, with its files, and the `coordinator` skill picks each worker's slice of it, so that the dependency runs one way and a worker never needs the `coordinator` skill. How a Claude Code session behaves (long commands, waits, interrupts, the permission check) belongs in `fortress-repo`, which every worker has loaded, not in a skill of its own; what only the coordinator needs of it goes to `coordinator`. The checker count and the distance are the ladder's metrics: the workflow's prompts say how to run them and the `coordinator` skill names them; `fortress-repo` holds nothing of them. `fortress-repo` carries no batch structure, on purpose: which roles exist, who builds, checks, runs the gate, commits and pushes to `main` are set by whoever writes the workflow or the brief, so that agents designing a workflow from the skill are not steered toward ours; the skill says how to do each thing, and the brief says which an agent does. The role split may later be written as behaviours a batch's instructions point to, in a skill of its own. An agent acts on its brief alone: the skill names no other authority over what it commits or pushes, and no rule an agent cannot act on (it cannot ask him). A worker works with three things, its brief, the record and the original tree, in one of two modes: building, where it stands on the record and carries out its mission, and exploring, where it has met something the record does not settle (a gap, two of the team's sources in conflict, new evidence against a decision), gathers evidence in the record first and then in the original tree, adds what it found to the record and returns to building. Where the team's sources disagree, the later one wins, the specification included. A worker never settles such a conflict itself, and never revises the specification to a later source on its own reading: the conflict is surfaced, and the curator rules after research by the nine steps; a decision on record is carried out, and questioned only on evidence the decision did not use. A conflict between the text and an implementation that no decision settles gets a ledger row and a test of the current behaviour; an `XXX` test belongs to repair work, where the current behaviour is tolerated for a time on purpose and the test is promoted once the fix is in. What a worker builds on while its question waits for him is left unsaid: it is case by case, and a reversible choice takes the path of least resistance without a rule. An agent takes the tree it starts from as green, starts with its own failing test, reuses only what its brief cites or its own work ran, and runs more only where its edit reaches; test first applies to an edit of source code. A point a brief wants reviewed is a "point to report", never a "stop", which reads as a condition that stops the worker. A skill's parts are written by the seven writing principles (`explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`), which he has read and judged safe to apply to every rewrite: the writer applies them to a whole part at once, and he then reads it, not comment by comment. The earlier lenses note and the review-style profile are not a writer's brief. Before he reads a rewritten part, a cold reader given only the skill reads it as the workers who use it would, flags each passage that would send it wrong or make it search, with its confidence, the undefined terms and the gotchas; the coordinator reviews the findings, the writer fixes them with his comments so far, and only then does he read it. A comment on the review page marks a problem area, not a sentence to patch: the fix is made at the level of its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind. The skills are rewritten in place, git holding the earlier text. One writer does the writing, briefed by the coordinator, every comment fix on the page among its tasks, made from the coordinator's brief of his comment instead of the coordinator interpreting his words: it edits the skill files and commits them, and the coordinator keeps the review page in step, so that the writer's context holds only the writing. The writer is a headless Claude session (`explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`, its standing brief `explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md`), since such a session keeps its prompt cache for an hour, as the coordinating session does, while an Agent-tool subagent keeps it for five minutes and so writes its whole context again when the curator's next comment comes later than that; the cache's one-hour writes cost more and are worth it. It is resumed for each writing task, and started fresh with only its standing brief when its history no longer serves, as after a large pass or the coordinator's compaction. Its standing order: ASD-STE100 at least halfway, terms defined first and then used, concise procedures, positive phrasing; and it does not take the register of what it reads, since FACTS, POSITIONS and many notes were written by earlier models in agent shorthand that the curator cannot follow cold, and the coordinator, which carries them in context, keeps drifting into it. A writer's minor decisions not taken are settled by the coordinator from the record, as his executive assistant, and not put to him; he is asked only where a rule would change its meaning or a new rule would enter. A position's bold title here is the record's handle, not his words, and is never quoted to him as his. A glossary of terms, in a skill or on a page, is written as a dictionary is: each term and the noun phrase that opens its definition with no article ("revival", not "the revival").
- **The statement for the public record on the usage limit.** "let the public record state that I'm now doing unpaid testing job of Anthropic's cloud infrastructure in my open source repository that is normally doing open source research of agentic coding capabilities." The account's weekly limit on all models stopped a running batch after its rung workers; later turns and subagents were served while the limit still read reached; he did not activate the promotional credit the panel offered, and his reading since is that visiting its page activated it unknowingly and that the work served was the $250 promotional credit for the cloud product, support having told him the offer had expired, "which was not true" (`coordinator/usage-metering-2026-09-30.md`, "After the report"); the container was booted afresh at each wake once nothing kept the session busy; at his word the batch was resumed to see whether it survives such interruptions and finishes.

## How he wants to be spoken to

- **The register.** "Drop the smart Alec essayist register before I blow a fuse": plain sentences, no framing flourishes, no closing lines that sum up in a phrase; advice as instructions, not as observations; replies very brief, plain English, no internal jargon. A wall of text is one he cannot absorb; the failure mode "is focused on over-compressing into a clever turn of phrase, but utterly fails in communicating clearly." Label which part answers which question when several are asked; do not restate what is in this file or in FACTS.md; when a concept is new to him, define it (he asked for reshape, ravel, planes, gather, outer product, Ring, Field, nat parameters, matrix multiplication).
- **Asks and decisions.** Decisions are presented one at a time as: what we do, what it changes, with a default he can accept without reading the argument; the argument lives in the committed review, not in chat. An ask for a yes states, in the message itself, what the worker would do, what it produces, what it touches in the tree, what it costs, what the yes commits him to afterwards and what a no costs ("What are the consequences of the yeses? What does that work even want to do? ... this is just pressuring me to give approval without understanding"); one ask per message; no label stands in for an explanation, and a new name is defined in the sentence that uses it; the recommendation comes after the explanation, in one line, never instead of it.
- **Ownership.** "I need to maintain some ownership of this work, even if we are doing agentic coding … I did not know what you did. I need to know what you did. And I need to be aware of those choices and decisions because I am the one carrying the responsibility for the consequences as a director of this revival": every re-approval row is gone through in detail, grouped by theme, and the count of reversals is not the measure. A decision made inside a worker's report and recorded in one line is a decision not made; flag it to him at the time.
- **The coordinator's standing goal** is to model what Pavol already knows and where his context has gaps, and to fill those gaps with the minimal set of relevant facts at the level he needs to decide; machine tokens are spent on thinking so that human context is protected. This came out of a compaction that left him "out of control, unaware of crucial details" while the coordinator was "taking unauthorized initiative which compounded my sense of helplessness to steer the Fortress revival efforts". The coordinator's two hats: "executive assistant here in this Fortress Revival project, helping me, the director, find a way forward, and the analyst that finds out what the fuck happened, why, and how do we move forward".
- **While a batch runs**, no progress reports on it until it lands. He is on Central European time; check-in times are given to him in UTC and in his local time. The harness's stop-hook reminders about uncommitted or unpushed work are processed silently, declined without a word while work is in flight, and never mentioned to him. He reads on an iOS client that sometimes shows stale state; "is anything in flight" is answered from the tree, not from the UI.
- **Format.** "table formatted in this way is hard to read on mobile … we just need a list": no tables in chat, lists. "write the numbers just as K or M. I'm fine as a programmer understanding what a kilo is": never spelled-out thousands and millions, and a numbers message carries few numbers, each with its meaning. Time is spoken from the clock or the record (when a batch will probably land, when a check-in fires), never from feel, "yesterday", "this morning", "last night", when the events were minutes or hours apart (protocol § 3). On his phone he reads a page while iOS's Speak reads it aloud at a fast rate, so every page for him has a Select button beside each larger section's heading that selects that section's text for Speak; a section's evidence and references are gathered at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points, and the Select button leaves them out, so that listening never runs through citations.

content.content:
- **A boot after a compaction costs about 285K tokens of context, and `FACTS.md` is about two fifths of it** does not hold: a boot costs about 250K of context, and `FACTS.md` is about a third of it (session `fe616d40`'s main transcript, each read's tokens the growth of the next call's prompt). The first call after the compaction is about 74K: the fixed part (system prompt, tools, skills, memory), about 56K read from the cache, and the compaction summary with the text the harness re-injects after it, about 18K written. The boot's reads then add `FACTS.md` about 88K (220 KB, read in five pages of about 45 KB, since the Read tool's page holds 25K tokens), `INDEX.md` 45K, `POSITIONS.md` 22K, the README and the protocol about 6K, and the handover's first section and the boot note about 14K; while a batch runs, its record's sections for Pavol and its journal add about 14K. Every read is written to the cache, so a boot writes about 195K, about 210K while a batch runs. A read costs about 2.5 bytes of file per token for `FACTS.md`, 2.7 for `INDEX.md` and 3.0 for `POSITIONS.md`, denser than prose because of paths, line numbers and code, so an estimate of a boot from file sizes uses these figures. `/context` shows the last call's prompt plus about 0.5K.

- **Stopping a turn kills every background agent alive at that moment; a message sent while the coordinator is busy kills nothing** (`coordinator/interrupt-archaeology/judgement.md` § 1, from `coordinator/interrupt-archaeology/evidence.md`; session `fe616d40`, main transcript, `subagents/` and `subagents/workflows/`; session `bdff267d`, `transcripts` branch, `001.jsonl`). The kill is the turn interrupt the transcript records as "[Request interrupted by user]", with any tool still in flight recorded "User rejected tool use": in the four interrupts that met live background agents all seven agents alive died at that instant, Workflow agents and `Agent`-tool workers alike, and none ever survived one. Eleven messages and three `/context` commands sent while the coordinator was busy, during five live runs, killed nothing: each was queued and delivered inside the running turn or as the next turn. Five manual compactions between turns killed nothing either. That the stop button sent the interrupt is confirmed for one case in Pavol's words and very likely for another (the iOS client's stop control under his right thumb), not shown for a third; the transcripts record the effect, not the control. Not tested: an automatic compaction mid-turn, and an interrupt during the Stop hook while a run is alive. The rule: send messages at any time; compact between turns; do not stop a turn while the session is working, including the seconds after a reply while the transcript backup runs; after an accidental stop, say so and the run is resumed with `resumeFromRunId`, which keeps every agent that had finished (the next entry; POSITIONS, "Check-ins and stops"). An `Agent`-tool worker killed by an interrupt cannot be resumed: a `SendMessage` to it is refused ("was stopped by the user and won't be resumed ... only launch a new agent if the user explicitly asks"), so it is relaunched only at Pavol's explicit ask, the new worker told its predecessor's leftovers (session `fe616d40`, six workers stopped by one interrupt). A Fable worker told to read its predecessor's transcript was ended by the API's safety filter as it printed the transcript's tail (`reasoning_extraction`, the false positive of the `agent()` entry below), so a Fable worker is given the leftovers in the tree and no transcript.
- **A restart of the session's own process kills its background runs, and `resumeFromRunId` then recovers every agent that had finished** (session `fe616d40`; the environment manager's log `/tmp/env-manager.log`). A restart of the session's process (`environment-manager task-run … --session-mode resume`), whether the platform's cap ("The platform stops the session's process ..." below) or a VM restart (the VM entry above), stops every Workflow run, every `Agent`-tool worker and the push loop alive at that moment. The conversation, the session ID, worktrees, untracked files, transcripts and each run's journal survive, and so do shell scripts the workers had started in the background. So the run is resumed, not relaunched: the same script and arguments as at its launch, with `resumeFromRunId`. A finished agent's result is kept, an unfinished one runs from its start, and its worktree's leftovers are its starting point; a relaunch from the base restarts at the first stage instead. An `Agent`-tool worker continues from its transcript on a `SendMessage`. The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of the run's `agent()` calls in call order, so it needs the launch's arguments byte for byte and the same order of calls: the base given as a short hash where the launch gave the full hash misses the cache from the first call, and when cached stages resolve at once a pipeline may call its next stage in another order than the live run did and miss from there. A run whose script has changed since launch is resumed from a copy of the script as launched (`git show <base>:<path>`); where the call order would differ, from a copy that forces the live run's order, prompts unchanged, wrapping `agent()` so that the finished calls are issued in the journal's order of their `started` lines (`RESUME_ORDER` and `orderedAgent`; the worked examples were copies made in the session's scratchpad, outside the repository, `wf-6.5-run1-resume.js`, `wf-N-run1-resume.js` and `wf-N-run1-land-first-gate.js`, and the scratchpad does not keep them). A copy that changes only what follows the cached prefix (a gate skipped, a commit's prompt extended) runs the changed call live and nothing before it. A stage stopped mid-work can leave its work in the tree: a commit stage killed before it had committed leaves its edits in the main tree, uncommitted, and a resume whose commit prompt names them (a changed prompt, so a new key) checks and keeps them and lands the batch; a gather killed mid-work leaves partial staged state, stashed and moved aside before the resume, and the gather runs again live from its start under its key, the journal then holding two `gather` lines under one `launched` line (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-6.5b/RECORD.md`, "A relaunched gather"). The run's journal is `journal.jsonl` in `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/`: one `launched` line, then a `started` line per agent call (`key`, `agentId`, `label`, `phase`) and a `result` line with the same key and the agent's structured result, none for an agent that returned nothing; a resumed run appends to the same journal, and an agent run live again under a key the journal holds gets a second `started` line (`coordinator/tools/journal-text.py`, which reads it). What does not carry over is a new session: `remote-container.md` § The 2026-09-18 restart and step 5 of the recovery list.

    b=len(re.findall(r'\bBuilt\b',l))
    if cs: cnt_e+=1; cnt_c+=len(cs); pf.append((i,title(l)[:70],cs))

    if b and cs: built_facts+=1

EOF
